title: The Work of Keeping a Public Building Public: The Drill Hall in Johannesburg
text:
The Work of Keeping a Public Building Public: The Drill Hall in Johannesburg

What happens to a building after the architecture is finished? For buildings intended to serve the public, their continued life depends on more than the physical conditions of their construction. It involves the activities that take place within them, the relationships they allow to develop, the people who occupy and shape them, and the institutional structures responsible for their upkeep. Yet these conditions are not always secured through the act of building itself. They are continually negotiated, often through forms of work that remain outside the conventional understanding of architectural practice.

title: Villa Sahar / Mahfoud Laasri Architecte - MLA
text:
Villa Sahar / Mahfoud Laasri Architecte - MLA

Sahar is a private residence in Casablanca conceived around the interplay of mass and lightness, materiality and transparency, and architecture and landscape. Its name, derived from the Arabic word سَحَر, refers to the moment just before dawn. The principal facade faces east, making morning light an essential part of the project's identity and an inspiration for its architectural expression.

title: The Vineyard HOUSE? / Lauti Esain
text:
The Vineyard HOUSE? / Lauti Esain

The Vineyard ?HOUSE? On September 10, 2022, at 12:29 p.m., I broke ground with the first of thousands of shovels I would dig to build my house. But the story began in my second year of architecture school, when I lost my parents. That was when I started working and saving, just in case something happened to me. Then, a dream emerged: to live on a vineyard. I decided that if I didn't need to use those savings upon graduating, I would use them to build my house. When I graduated, my savings were enough for 215 sq ft (20 m²), but by building it with my own hands, I could save on labor costs and reach 355 sq ft (33 m²).

The compact plot sits within a dense piece of urban fabric, surrounded on all sides by neighbouring houses. Its shape is skewed. The project begins with the challenge of inscribing a house into this distorted figure. The longest wall of the plot becomes the guide. From it, a set of geometric rules gradually unfolds, quietly organising the plan.

Set on a long, gentle slope in the foothills of the Catskill Mountains, Understory House takes its name from its precise position within the forest—neither rooted on the forest floor nor lifted above the canopy, but suspended in between, where the midstory becomes the primary experience. Located in a rural second-growth forest marked by miles of historic stone walls, the 3,170-square-foot house responds directly to the character and memory of the land.

title: Beyond Buildings: ArchDaily's November Editorial Focus
text:
Beyond Buildings: ArchDaily's November Editorial Focus

"Design a cultural center on a desert coastline, in the style of Alvar Aalto, wood structure, golden hour, aerial drone shot, photorealistic, 4K." Within seconds, a line like this returns a convincing image. What is less visible is the shift it demands. For centuries, architectural imagination relied on the body: the hand that sketches, the fingers that shape a model, or, more recently, the click of a mouse in computational tools. Words came afterward, to explain what had already taken form. Today, the order is increasingly reversed. Before an image can exist, it must first be described: its references named, its materials listed, its mood specified.

title: A Walk on the Roof: Linnahall and Tallinn’s Shifting Shoreline
text:
A Walk on the Roof: Linnahall and Tallinn’s Shifting Shoreline

From the end of Mere Boulevard in Tallinn, Linnahall appears as a long, low mass of limestone and concrete laid between the Old Town and the bay, kept deliberately beneath the line of the medieval silhouette so that the spires remain visible from the water. Broad stairways climb its flanks to a roof paved as a public square, and from there a sequence of terrace steps down toward a small pier, a helicopter pad and the open Gulf of Finland. Under that surface sit an amphitheater for 4,200 people, a foyer of 6,000 square meters, an ice hall, cafés, a bowling alley and a recording studio.

title: Sharjah Design Centre Unveils Plans for Rammed Earth Building Opening in 2029
text:

Sharjah Design Centre (SDC), a new institution dedicated to design, material research, prototyping, and production, is scheduled to open in 2029 as part of the Sharjah Creative Quarter in the United Arab Emirates. Designed by Taller de Arquitectura – Mauricio Rocha in collaboration with architect Daniel Rosselló, the centre will bring together specialist laboratories, research facilities, production spaces, and public programmes within a purpose-built building. Under the leadership of H.E. Sheikha Hind bint Majid Al Qasimi, SDC aims to connect designers, manufacturers, researchers, and entrepreneurs through an integrated framework for material experimentation, fabrication, and knowledge exchange.

title: Designing Furniture to Outlast the Fit-Out
text:
Designing Furniture to Outlast the Fit-Out

Furniture waste is not always the result of physical damage that renders a product unusable. Chairs, sofas, and tables are often discarded because they no longer fit an interior concept, are perceived as outdated, or are replaced during a renovation. In many cases, their structures remain functional, even when upholstery is worn, or the surrounding space has changed. The result is a cycle of replacement in which usable products become waste, while new resources are extracted and processed to manufacture their successors.

title: Lacaton & Vassal Receives the 2027 Charlotte Perriand Award
text:
Lacaton & Vassal Receives the 2027 Charlotte Perriand Award

Pritzker Prize laureates Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal have been announced as the recipients of the 2027 Le Prix Charlotte Perriand. Organized annually by the Créateurs Design Awards (CDA), the prize recognizes practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design through a peer-led voting process. For its eighth edition, the organization highlighted the work of the French architectural studio as a demonstration of "how the adaptation of existing structures can improve living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage." Previous recipients of the prize include Xu Tiantian; Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa; Frida Escobedo; and Jeanne Gang.

title: Architecture and Neurodivergence: Designing for Different Ways of Perceiving Space
text:
Architecture and Neurodivergence: Designing for Different Ways of Perceiving Space

Wide doorways, properly designed ramps, and elevators are essential to a building's accessibility. But whether people can actually use its spaces also depends on the sensory conditions they offer. For some neurodivergent people, this is critical, as bright lights, overlapping sounds, or confusing circulation routes can prevent them from staying in a space and participating in activities.

title: House in Dahiya / Studio Toggle
text:
House in Dahiya / Studio Toggle

House in Dahiya gives nothing to the street. On a quiet road in Dahiyat Abdullah Al Salem, one of central Kuwait City's most premium residential districts, a stepped mass of raw exposed concrete rises between two date palms. Its principal facades are closed, and the entrance sits back behind dark vertical fins. The brief asked for exactly this: a house closed and unreadable from the street, yet open, light and generous within, and able to withstand Kuwait's heat, dust and salt air with little upkeep. Behind the sealed mass lies a protected inner world with its own climate, color and calm.

title: Everyone is building AI agents. Who’s designing the stop button?
text:
Everyone is building AI agents. Who’s designing the stop button?

We used to design predictable user flows. Now AI can interpret, decide, and act on its own. Here’s why the hardest design decisions happen where that autonomy ends.

In September 2025, researchers at Thinking Machines Lab ran the same prompt through a language model 1,000 times. They set the temperature to zero, a setting that should, in theory, make token selection deterministic.

They got 80 different completions from the same prompt, model, and settings.

What’s even more interesting is that all 1,000 outputs were identical for the first 102 tokens. The differences started at token 103, when the model described where Richard Feynman was born.

The researchers traced the variation to how computations were performed under different server batching conditions. With a modified implementation, they eventually got all 1,000 outputs to match.

Their research demonstrated something important. Even when you try to make a language model behave predictably, the infrastructure running it can introduce variation.

Now imagine building a product on top of that model. One that creates freight bookings, updates customer records, or moves medical documents between systems.

The problem isn’t that AI can produce different answers. That’s often exactly why we’re using it.

The problem starts when those answers turn into actions, and nobody has decided which parts of the process are allowed to be unpredictable.

For decades, we designed software around the assumption that we knew what would happen next. AI is making that assumption increasingly difficult to maintain. And I think a lot of early-stage teams are still designing as if nothing has changed.

—

We used to know what would happen next

Think about how we’ve designed digital products for the last few decades.

You open an app, select something, complete a form, click a button, and move to the next step. The interface responds according to predefined rules.

A flight booking is a good example. Select your destination, choose a date, pick a flight, enter passenger details, pay, and receive confirmation.

There might be hundreds of conditions behind that experience, but the designer and engineering team can define them in advance. If the payment fails, show an error. If a seat is unavailable, offer another. If information is missing, ask the user to complete it.

This is the thinking that shaped most of our design tools and methods. User flows, wireframes, journey maps, information architecture, design systems, and interactive prototypes.

We design states and transitions between them. We decide what happens when someone clicks a button, makes a mistake, or returns to an unfinished process.

Traditional software was never perfectly deterministic. Search results changed, recommendations were personalized, and external services could fail. But the core behavior of most transactional interfaces was defined by explicit rules.

The designer didn’t need to know which flight someone would book. They needed to know how booking a flight worked.

What’s interesting is that the idea of software moving beyond explicit commands is not new. In 1993, Jakob Nielsen wrote about noncommand user interfaces. He described systems that could infer what users wanted instead of requiring them to communicate everything through specific commands. That was more than 30 years ago.

We’ve been imagining software that understands intention for decades. We just couldn’t build many of those experiences in a commercially practical way.

Now we can and that changes what it means to design a user flow.

—

The user no longer has to define every step

Imagine you’re designing a reporting tool.

Previously, a user would select data, configure filters, choose a report format, generate the report, and download it. The interface existed to collect instructions.

Today, someone can simply write: “Tell me why our conversion dropped last month and what we should investigate.”

The product can interpret the request, retrieve information, compare periods, identify patterns, and decide how to present the findings.

We removed five steps from the interface, but we introduced a completely different kind of complexity.

What if the data is incomplete? What if two dashboards define conversion differently? What if the AI produces a convincing explanation that is actually incorrect?

A traditional user flow doesn’t fully capture these possibilities because the system can now make decisions about how to approach the task.

This is also where the difference between AI adoption and actual automation becomes interesting.

According to the 2026 Stanford AI Index, 88% of surveyed organizations reported using AI in 2025, up from 55% in 2023. Yet scaled AI agent deployment remained in the single digits across nearly all business functions.

Companies are using AI, but letting it run meaningful business processes is a very different challenge.

There’s a big difference between asking AI to draft an email and allowing it to send that email to 4,000 customers.

This is where UX becomes much more important than simply making the interface look intelligent.

—

Non-deterministic vs deterministic

I think it’s worth clarifying the terminology because we tend to mix these things together.

A deterministic system follows predefined logic. Given the same relevant input and state, the same rules produce the same output.

A non-deterministic system can produce different outcomes under apparently identical conditions. With generative AI, it’s often more useful to talk about probabilistic behavior, interpretation, and uncertainty.

Think about the difference between validating an email address and understanding what an email means.

Checking whether an email address has the correct format is a deterministic task.

Understanding whether an incoming message is a complaint, a booking request, or a pricing enquiry requires interpretation.

Now connect that interpretation to an actual workflow.

If the AI decides it’s a booking request, it might create a shipment. If it decides it’s a complaint, it might escalate the issue. If it identifies a pricing enquiry, it might prepare a quotation.

The user didn’t explicitly select a workflow. The system did.

So yes, the output might be non-deterministic UI. The wording changes, the content changes, and sometimes even the structure of what appears on the screen changes.

But the bigger problem is UX.

Users need to understand what the system is doing, predict the consequences of their actions, correct mistakes, and know when they can trust an outcome.

You can design a beautiful AI interface with great typography, smooth animations, and perfectly polished chat components. But if the underlying system makes decisions users cannot understand or correct, the experience is broken.

The difficult part is designing what the product is allowed to do with that response.

—

The biggest mistake is making everything non-deterministic

There’s an assumption that the more autonomous an AI product becomes, the better it is.

Why ask people to complete forms when AI can understand them? Why use predefined workflows when an agent can decide what to do?

Those are reasonable questions. But just because AI can interpret information doesn’t mean it should be responsible for executing every resulting action.

And just because a product uses AI doesn’t mean everything inside it has to behave probabilistically.

In fact, some of the more interesting AI products are doing the opposite. They’re deliberately combining deterministic and non-deterministic systems, deciding exactly where each one should take control.

A lot of failures come from making something non-deterministic that should have been a form.

This is especially relevant for early-stage founders. It’s tempting to turn every interaction into a prompt because it makes the product feel more advanced.

But sometimes a form, a predefined workflow, or a simple confirmation button is exactly what the experience needs.

Two products illustrate this particularly well.

—

Routine Labs: Let AI build the workflow, not improvise while running it

Routine Labs works on automating processes inside existing legacy software, particularly in healthcare. Its approach is interesting because AI is used to help build automations, while production execution follows deterministic workflows.

Imagine a medical practice dealing with documents across several applications. A blood test arrives and needs to be identified, checked against patient consent, and uploaded to Germany’s electronic patient record, known as the ePA.

Traditionally, someone has to move between systems, find the correct information, check the necessary conditions, and complete the process manually.

A fully autonomous AI agent could attempt to interpret and navigate that process every time.

Routine takes a different approach.

According to the company, its hybrid engine uses generative AI to create automations, but the workflows running in production follow repeatable, logged logic. On its healthcare website, Routine also states that it doesn’t use AI during production operations or transfer personal data to LLMs.

That’s a very deliberate product decision. The uncertainty is concentrated in building the automation, where the process can be defined and checked. Production execution is designed to be predictable.

Now think about what that means for UX.

The user doesn’t necessarily need a conversation with an agent. They need to know what automation is running, which steps have been completed, whether the correct document was processed, and whether something requires their attention.

Routine’s public product examples show exactly this type of workflow: search for blood tests, check ePA consent, and upload the document.

The interface can communicate progress and exceptions through familiar patterns such as status indicators, execution histories, and review steps. No chatbot required.

And that’s what makes this approach interesting. The intelligence is used where it adds value, without making the entire experience dependent on the model interpreting the process correctly every single time.

Routine is an example of how you can build an AI-native product while keeping its actual execution deterministic.

—

Zauber: Let AI handle ambiguity, but make uncertainty visible

Zauber approaches the same problem from a different direction.

It builds AI agents for sea and air freight forwarding, working inside existing tools such as Outlook and integrating with systems like CargoWise.

Freight forwarding is an interesting environment for AI because so much operational work depends on interpreting unstructured information.

Emails, PDFs, packing lists, changing shipment details, special instructions, and incomplete documents. Information comes from different sources and doesn’t always agree.

An operator might receive an email requesting a shipment booking, with a packing list attached and a delivery date changed somewhere in the conversation.

Traditionally, someone would read everything, interpret the request, check the details, and manually enter the information into the booking system.

Zauber uses AI to handle much of that interpretation.

Its agents can read rate requests, identify relevant shipment details, retrieve rates, and prepare quotations for review. For booking creation, they can extract information from emails and documents and populate the necessary fields in CargoWise.

But the most interesting part is how the product handles information it cannot verify.

According to Zauber’s product page, if a declared value is missing or the volume doesn’t match the packing list, the system flags the discrepancy rather than guessing. The operator confirms the information before the booking is created.

Imagine the email says a shipment has a volume of 58.4 m³, while the packing list says 60.03 m³.

The AI has already completed most of the work, but the interface should make that disagreement visible, show where the information came from, and let the operator resolve it.

Instead of asking the user to complete every field, the product directs their attention to the two fields that matter. That’s a different way of designing workflows.

And there’s another detail I like about Zauber. Its product documentation describes monitoring agent sessions, including where the workflow hands control back to a human operator. The handover itself becomes something the company can observe, measure, and improve.

Routine and Zauber use different architectures, but they make a similar decision. They don’t treat autonomy as an all-or-nothing feature.

They decide where the AI should interpret information, where deterministic rules should take over, and when the user needs to step in.

—

Why a great AI demo can become a terrible product

Here’s a simple calculation that explains why these decisions matter.

Imagine a workflow with ten steps. Each step has a 95% chance of completing correctly, and all ten steps must succeed. Assuming the outcomes are independent, the probability of the entire workflow succeeding is:

A workflow that’s 95% reliable at each individual step could succeed end to end only about 60% of the time.

This is a simplified example, not a measured AI failure rate. Real systems have dependencies, validation, retries, and recovery mechanisms that change the result. But it illustrates why model accuracy alone isn’t a sufficient product metric.

An AI might extract information correctly most of the time. What happens when it doesn’t? What if an incorrect value gets passed to another system? What if an action succeeds but the confirmation fails? What happens if the agent repeats the action and creates a duplicate?

A lot of products look great because we’ve designed and tested the successful version.

The first time the model gets confused, the actual product experience begins. That’s where traditional design tools start showing their limitations.

A Figma prototype is excellent for representing predefined states. It’s not particularly good at representing a distribution of possible outputs, variable execution paths, or a failure that happens once in 50 runs.

This doesn’t make Figma irrelevant. It means static screens are no longer enough to validate the behavior we’re designing.

—

What happens when we ignore this?

One common failure is the illusion of completion.

An agent says it updated a record, sent an email, or created a booking. But perhaps it only prepared the action. Maybe an API failed. Maybe the system saved the wrong information.

If the interface displays the model’s response as proof that the action succeeded, the user has no reliable way to know what happened.

Another is hidden uncertainty. Information extracted from a document might appear exactly like verified information retrieved from a database. The interface gives both the same visual weight, even though one is an interpretation and the other is an authoritative value.

Then there’s the opposite problem: excessive human supervision.

Some products solve uncertainty by asking users to approve absolutely everything. But if someone has to review 100 decisions and 98 are consistently correct, they eventually stop paying attention.

You’ve automated the original work and replaced it with a new job: supervising the automation.

That’s not necessarily a better product.

There’s also the problem of incorrect decisions spreading through otherwise reliable systems. An AI might identify the wrong customer, after which every deterministic step executes perfectly while updating the wrong records.

The system worked exactly as designed, but the business outcome was wrong.

It takes us to the point when designing error states isn’t enough. We need to design the relationship between interpretation, verification, execution, and recovery.

—

How I approach designing this in an early-stage team

Working on a new AI product today, I’d start by mapping the workflow into three categories: deterministic, fuzzy, and irreversible.

It’s a simple exercise, but it forces you to make decisions that are easy to ignore when you’re focused on the demo.

Deterministic steps are operations with clear rules. Validating required fields, checking permissions, retrieving records, and preventing duplicate actions. These should generally be handled through conventional software.

Fuzzy steps require interpretation. Reading an email, understanding a document, classifying a request, or drafting a response. This is where AI becomes useful.

Irreversible or high-impact steps are actions with meaningful consequences. Sending an external email, issuing a payment, changing a sensitive record, or committing a booking. These need explicit permission boundaries, verification, and, where appropriate, human approval.

Once you’ve mapped those steps, a lot of product decisions become clearer. You can decide where the model is actually needed, what the interface needs to communicate, and which actions should never happen silently.

The next thing I’d do is stop treating the AI output as the interface itself. For many B2B products, I’d rather have the model return structured information and let deterministic components render it.

If an agent extracts booking information, the user should see a normal booking interface, not a paragraph explaining what the model found. The model fills in the card. It doesn’t need to invent the card.

Let’s take something everyone understands. Booking a flight.

You ask an AI assistant to book an early flight to Lisbon on Friday for you and Ania, returning Sunday evening.

First, the fuzzy part. The model has to interpret what “early” and “evening” mean, figure out which Ania you’re talking about, and make a few assumptions based on your previous bookings.

Instead of giving you a long chat response, the UI presents a structured draft. You can see what the model understood, where each assumption came from, and correct anything that looks wrong. Nothing has been booked yet.

Then comes deterministic validation. The system checks actual flight availability, passenger details, fare conditions, and prices against the airline’s data and predefined rules.

Everything checks out. Two seats are available, the refundable fare costs €398, and it’s within your budget. The interface shows a verified booking summary, without making you go through every individual check.

Now the interesting part.

You click Book, but the refundable fare sells out before the booking is completed. The only remaining option is €342, but it’s non-refundable.

Technically, it’s cheaper. It even passes your budget limit. But it’s not what you originally agreed to.

This is where the interface needs to change. Instead of letting the agent choose the cheaper ticket, the UI explains what happened, keeps all the information that’s still valid, and asks whether you want to book the non-refundable fare or look for another option.

Looking at the entire flow, the interesting part is how the boundaries change. The model can interpret the request, but it can’t set prices or book anything. Rules and live systems handle validation. And when the refundable fare suddenly becomes unavailable, the system stops and hands the decision back to the user.

Here’s how those boundaries work across the same booking:

One booking, three different levels of autonomy. The system can interpret, validate, and prepare actions, but the rules for handing control back to the user change depending on the consequences.

This is why I don’t think we can design AI workflows as just a sequence of predetermined screens anymore.

The same task moves between interpretation, validation, and execution. A decision that seemed straightforward a moment ago can suddenly require human judgment.

And the interface has to handle that without making someone start the whole process again.

There’s no need to show confidence scores or explain every decision the model makes. Show the assumptions when they matter, keep routine checks in the background, and make the consequences clear when something changes.

The difficult part is designing the transition between them.

—

Prototype the behavior, not just the happy path

I’d also move to working prototypes earlier.

Tools like Cursor, Lovable, v0, and Claude Code make it easier to build interfaces connected to actual model behavior. You can still start in Figma, but at some point you need to see the variability rather than imagine it.

Run the same scenario repeatedly. Try different phrasing. Use incomplete documents. Give the system conflicting instructions. Turn the failures into evaluation cases.

Anthropic’s research on building effective agents makes a useful distinction between predefined workflows and agents that dynamically decide their own steps. It also recommends starting with the simplest architecture that can solve the problem.

Not everything needs an agent. Sometimes a fixed workflow with one intelligent step is more useful, less expensive, and significantly easier to test.

For the actual implementation, structured outputs, schemas, state machines, execution logs, and human approval mechanisms help make these boundaries real. Tools like LangGraph and LangSmith can support stateful workflows, tracing, and evaluation.

None of these tools eliminates model uncertainty. They help you design a product that knows what to do when uncertainty appears.

Finally, I’d measure something more useful than how often the AI completes a task. I’d measure how much human attention the workflow requires.

Things like:
How often does someone need to correct the output? How long do those corrections take? How often does the agent require intervention? How many tasks actually finish correctly without creating additional work?

An agent that automates 80% of a process but makes the remaining 20% painful may not save much time. The goal is reducing the total effort needed to achieve a reliable outcome.

—

The hardest decision is how much control to give away

For founders, this is where UX becomes product strategy.

Give AI too little autonomy and you’ve built an expensive assistant that still requires users to do all the work. Give it too much and users have to trust decisions they cannot inspect or predict.

There’s no universal answer because the consequences vary between workflows. Drafting an email is different from sending it. Preparing a booking is different from creating it. Extracting information from a medical document is different from modifying a patient record.

And the boundary isn’t necessarily permanent.

A workflow might begin with every action requiring approval. After hundreds of successful executions and measurable evidence of reliability, some steps can become automatic. Other steps might always require human involvement because the cost of a mistake is too high.

This also changes how I’d approach a zero-to-one product.

Instead of promising to automate an entire business operation, I’d start with one painful workflow, make it measurable, understand its exceptions, and gradually expand.

“Our AI handles your entire freight operation” might sound impressive.

“We turn incoming shipment requests into verified, ready-to-create bookings” is a much clearer product promise.

You can measure the time saved. You can understand what goes wrong. You can build trust before introducing more autonomy.

And for an early-stage startup, trust is a much more useful asset than an impressive demo.

—

Design the boundary, not just the flow

For decades, we focused on making software easier for people to navigate. We mapped their journeys, removed unnecessary steps, and made interfaces more predictable.

Now we’re increasingly designing software that navigates parts of the work on their behalf. We need to understand what the system knows, what it assumes, what it can verify, and what it’s allowed to do when information is incomplete.

We need to decide when the system should act, when it should ask, and when it should stop. And perhaps most importantly, we need to accept that not every part of an AI-native product benefits from more AI.

Sometimes the best decision is to let a model interpret something and hand execution to deterministic software.
Sometimes it’s to prepare an action and ask for confirmation.
Sometimes it’s to admit that there isn’t enough information to continue.

Routine Labs and Zauber are useful examples because they make those boundaries part of their product architecture rather than treating them as an afterthought.

The next generation of product design isn’t just about making interfaces more intelligent. It’s about deciding how much unpredictability the product can safely absorb.

If you’re a founder building in this space, take your most important workflow and mark every step as deterministic, fuzzy, or irreversible. You’ll probably discover more about the product you’re building than you would from another conversation about which AI model to use.

Your AI doesn’t need to behave the same way every time.
But your users need to know what they can depend on.

References

  • Thinking Machines Lab, Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (2025)
  • Stanford HAI, 2026 AI Index Report
  • Jakob Nielsen, Noncommand User Interfaces (1993)
  • Microsoft Research, Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (2019)
  • Anthropic, Building Effective Agents

title: I let AI build. I don’t let AI decide.
text:
I let AI build. I don’t let AI decide.

My list of tasks I give models without a second thought and what I review until the tools evolve.

I’ve used generative models for almost four years and designed machine learning applications for seven before that, so people ask what I delegate. I approach this as an apologist, someone who makes the case for the technology in the right context.

That’s generous, since an OpenAI model declared me dead in 2023.

As far as public reports available up to my latest update (October 2024), Patrick Neeman passed away in 2023. So there wouldn’t be 2025 UX activities or updates from him.
— GPT-5

The reality — I’m a data point of one, and everyone should use their own judgment to make the call, including you.

The usual split hands models rote work. Mine doesn’t: I hand over creative first drafts and keep models away from arithmetic and one-way-door analysis.

I focus on where the tools are dependable and where my judgment makes the final call.

Ethan Mollick showed why the split fails in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier (2023). Also, in a Boston Consulting Group experiment, consultants using GPT-4 finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with 40% higher quality. Outside the model’s reach, they did worse than people alone.

The edge is jagged, so difficulty misleads.

My test is the guideline, which is how I build trust in the results. Building work has a guideline outside itself: the page runs or the source checks out.

Deciding work writes the guideline and carries my signature.

Tasks I Give AI

Every task in this group has a check outside the work, so a wrong answer shows up in minutes. Even here, a human makes the final call.

Most of this work doesn’t have to be 100% right, and user experience has always worked that way, AI or not. We never fully know what’s going on in a user’s head, so we design from partial evidence, test, and adjust. A model’s first draft or prototype fits that habit, since it only has to be good enough to react to.

The reacting is the craft: educated guesses and judgment calls built on experience, and that taste can never come out of a model. Where it comes from is the subject of How we save entry-level UX work that teaches craft in the time of AI.

Research Topics

Marcia J. Bates described searching as berrypicking in The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface (1989). Each result changes the question, and the answer arrives in pieces.

This is foundational for how AI works today.

I used her ideas to frame search and summarization in legal tech software, and I still research that way.

Models make berrypicking faster, surfacing 20 sources while I’d still be reading my third. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, searching for answers topped the list of tasks respondents now do mostly with artificial intelligence tools, at 54.1%.

The model picks berries fast, and I still decide which ones are ripe.

The source itself is the guideline: every candidate can be opened and read, so a bad suggestion costs me a minute.

The Cognitive Models of Information Retrieval entry on UX Guidelines argues that answers should keep the trail visible. I wrote about the structure underneath that trail in Information architecture is the foundation AI is starving for.

Because of this, I write to learn and to codify what I think, so reading the sources is where my thinking takes shape.

Generate Drafts

Most first drafts I publish now start with a model, written against my style rules, my notes, and an argument I’ve already chosen.

A model always needs that context, because a cold prompt gets you the average of the internet, which Scott Jenson called average design. Then I cut, reorder, and send back instructions like “merge and relength” until the piece says what I meant.

A draft has a guideline once the argument and the rules exist, and a script grades it against the rule file before I do.

The thesis stays mine, because a thesis has no guideline; it is the guideline.

A draft is cheap to replace, which frees me to treat the first one as raw material.

Because the draft carries my context, it makes me faster.

In Study finds ChatGPT boosts worker productivity for some writing tasks, MIT researchers reported that 453 professionals using ChatGPT in 2023 finished writing tasks 40% faster, with work rated 18% higher in quality.

What I like most is the surprise: a draft sometimes raises an angle I hadn’t thought of, and the best ones make the final piece.

Build Prototypes

I’ve always written code, from Perl sites and blogging software to the small tools I build now. Claude Code and Cursor write most of the code behind the Chrome extensions I ship at Extend Chrome and the icon reference at UX Icons.

I describe the behavior, read the diff, and click through the result. The browser enforces the guideline: a button either does what I asked or fails in plain view.

A prototype asks me to click, which beats trusting the model’s account of its own work.

Figma’s 2026 AI report found that the share of designers participating in development nearly doubled in a year, from 21% to 41%. What I hand over is the typing.

What the extension should do, and when it’s good enough to publish, stays with me.

Automate Repeat Work

Anything I do three times becomes a skill.

Anthropic describes skills in Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills as folders of instructions, scripts, and resources an agent loads when a task calls for them. I’ve written them for site uploads, release notes, and the CARE prompt behind this article.

Here the last good run is the guideline, since I can see which written step slipped.

Aviation learned this early and has refined it ever since.

In The Checklist, Walter J. Boyne recounts how the Boeing Model 299 crashed in 1935 with an experienced crew after its controls were left locked, and the Air Corps answered with checklists because the limit was human memory.

Counting is its own trap: Mollick notes that a model writes a fine sonnet but misses an exact 50-word poem, because it works in tokens.

Don’t ask a model to count. Ask it to write the thing that counts in a deterministic manner.

So a model wrote the script that checks every draft for word counts, banned words, and repeated phrases, and I wrote every rule it enforces.

Unlike a paper checklist, a skill can improve itself: my research and writing skills fold each correction back into their rules, and new rules wait for my approval.

Tasks I Keep Human in the Loop

These are 100% problems, and they’re the reason self-driving cars scare me, because it’s not just about the AI but about the humans around it.

A car that handles 99% of the road still meets the last 1% at road speed, with no undo. Some tasks are risky because other humans are involved, each making a judgment call no model can see inside. In 2018, an Uber test vehicle killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona, and CNN’s report on the Uber test driver’s 2023 guilty plea notes the safety driver had looked away for more than a third of the trip.

Before I’d hand any of these over, two conditions would have to hold:

  • Human in the loop: Review the work before it takes effect
  • Explainability: Understand how the model got there

A confident answer with no visible reasoning leaves me nothing to review. Tammy Snow makes the builder’s version of this case in AI Doesn’t Have a Technology Problem. It Has a Human One. She calls for transparent reasoning and reversible actions, because “the system doesn’t know what it doesn’t know,” and treats each override as feedback.

Dan Maccarone adds the reviewer’s side in We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us. One of his clients runs on the rule “people conclude, machines don’t,” and he warns that a reviewer who never overrules the machine is a rubber stamp.

Rubber stamps are dangerous, AI or not.

Make Financial Decisions

A large language model isn’t a large mathematical model: it predicts likely text, so even one that gets a sum right 95% of the time is wrong once in every 20 tries. For a draft, 95% is a good day, but for a calculation it isn’t good enough.

When I use a model for money at all, it writes the spreadsheet formulas, and the spreadsheet does the math.

Choosing what to do with the numbers stays with me.

The outcome shows up years later and turns on things a model can’t see, like how much risk I can live with.

In Gallup’s Where Americans and Canadians Turn for Financial Guidance (2026), 18% of U.S. adults seeking financial guidance in the past year had used artificial intelligence tools.

By contrast, 32% had at least some confidence in financial advisers.

Access My Sensitive Data

Customer contracts, personnel records, passwords, and anything a client trusted my team to protect never go into a model I don’t control. In legal tech, the contract data belonged to the customer, and that habit stuck.

Deciding who sees a record is a judgment call, and sending it has no undo. Depending on a tool’s terms, what I paste can end up in training data and surface later in someone else’s answer. In Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models (2020), researchers got GPT-2 to repeat memorized training text word for word, including names, phone numbers, and email addresses.

Once a record leaves the building, no review after the fact brings it back.

In IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report (2025), one in five organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI, meaning tools employees used without approval. Heavy shadow AI use added $670,000 to average breach costs.

Sensitive work stays in tools my company has approved and the vendors have locked down.

Get Psychological Advice

When I need advice about stress, a conflict at work, or my own state of mind, I go to people.

A model can explain burnout, since the literature offers a guideline. What to do about my own life depends on things I may not say out loud.

Models also lean toward agreeing with whoever is typing. In Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence (2025), researchers tested 11 leading models and found they affirmed users’ actions 50% more than humans did.

In a live experiment, people who got the flattering answers grew more convinced they were right and less willing to repair a conflict. They also rated the flattering answers higher.

Good advice sometimes tells you you’re wrong, and a model tuned to please rarely will.

A friend, a mentor, or a licensed therapist knows me over time and can push back when I’m the one causing the trouble.

Send Final Messages in My Name

A model can draft an email or a Slack reply, and I’ll edit it like any other draft. What it doesn’t get is the send button. A message to my team, my manager, or a customer carries my name and my relationships, and once it goes out, there’s no undo.

People can tell, and it costs something.

In Study uncovers social cost of using AI in conversations, Cornell University researchers paired 219 pairs of people in chats where smart replies were available.

When people believed their partner was leaning on the suggested replies, they rated that partner as less cooperative and felt less connected to them.

A message in my name is something I own, and a model can’t make promises for me.

Agents raise the stakes, since they can send on their own schedule, many times before anyone reads the log. So a model drafts, and I read, edit, and press send. The person on the other end is deciding whether to trust me.

Set Your Own Guidelines

The first group grows every few months as skills, scripts, and search tools improve. I’ll keep moving work across the line, and I’ll check each move by clicking, running, or reading.

The second group hasn’t moved, and I don’t expect it to.

Making financial decisions, guarding sensitive data, getting psychological advice, and sending final messages in my name have no guideline or can’t be undone.

So here’s the test I’d give any designer, product manager, or researcher sorting through their own week. Run each task through these three questions first:

  • Name the guideline. If nothing outside the work can check it, the task is a decision, so keep it, however good the model’s draft looks.
  • Check who wrote it. If you wrote the guideline yourself, hand the work over, then review everything that comes back against it.
  • Find the signature. If your name is on the result, or it must be right 100% of the time, keep the whole task yourself.

Your groups will probably look a little different from mine. That’s fine, as long as you can name the guideline for every job in the first one.

I let AI build. I don’t let AI decide. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Agents struggle with the same bad UX we do
text:
Agents struggle with the same bad UX we do

Computer-use agents can’t guess, improvise, or ask a coworker. That makes them the most honest usability testers we’ve ever had.

The first time I watched an agent fail on a vendor portal, I recognized the failure immediately. Not because I understood the model. Because I’d failed in exactly the same place myself.

For example, I watched a run where an agent reached a form that had two buttons labeled “Continue” and “Submit”, chose the wrong one, and the run stalled. This wasn’t the agent’s fault, it was bad UX.

I design products at Deck, where we build infrastructure for computer-use agents: software that logs into websites and operates them the way a person would, clicking, typing, and navigating. Most of the portals our agents work in were never designed to be automated. They’re utility accounts, vendor payment pages, and back-office tools with no API, built for humans and often barely built for those.

Watching thousands of agent runs across these portals has taught me something I didn’t expect. The places agents get stuck are almost never exotic. They’re the same places people get stuck. The difference is that people hide it.

Humans glance over bad design. Agents can’t.

Steve Krug observed years ago in Don’t Make Me Think that people rarely figure out how a website works. They muddle through: guessing, backtracking, and moving on once something seems to work. That muddling is a kind of invisible labor, and it hides an enormous amount of design debt.

When a button label is ambiguous, a person tries one and sees what happens. When a menu only appears on hover, a person waves the mouse around until it shows up. When a session expires halfway through a form, a person sighs, logs back in, and starts again. When they truly can’t work something out, they ask a coworker who learned the trick last month. None of this shows up in analytics as failure. It shows up as “time on task,” or not at all.

An agent can’t do most of that. It doesn’t remember the trick from last month. It can’t lean over and ask someone. It can retry, but it can’t intuit which of two identically labeled buttons the designer meant. So the debt that humans quietly absorb becomes visible, run after run, as a step that broke.

That’s what makes agents unusually honest testers. They don’t experience frustration, but they surface every place where a design depends on someone guessing right.

Where agents get stuck

The failures cluster into a handful of patterns. None of them will surprise a designer. That’s the point.

1. Labels that only make sense if you already know. “Manage,” “Edit,” and “Settings” all on one page. Icon-only buttons with no text. Two buttons that both say “Continue.” Don Norman’s idea of signifiers, the cues that tell you what an action will do, is the whole game here. When the signifier is missing, a person relies on memory or experimentation. An agent has neither.

2. State that hides. Menus that exist only on hover. Buttons that are disabled with no explanation of why. Status communicated purely by color. Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic, visibility of system status, was written for people. It turns out to be the first requirement for agents too. If the interface doesn’t say what state it’s in, nothing operating it can know.

3. Interruptions. The cookie banner, the “rate your experience” modal, the promotional interstitial that appears on the third visit, the chat widget that slides over the submit button. Every one of these is a small tax on human attention. For an agent, an unexpected overlay can be the end of the run. It’s a useful mirror: if an interruption is disruptive enough to stop a machine cold, it’s worth asking what it costs your users.

4. Time. Sessions that expire mid-task. One-time codes that time out before they arrive. Pages that log you out “for your security” during a multi-step process. People tolerate these grudgingly. For any automated or delegated work, they’re often the single largest source of failure, and they’re a sign that the system was designed around a single short visit, not around real work.

5. Success that doesn’t announce itself. This is the one I care about most, because it’s the one I spent years on in payments. You submit a payment and land back on the dashboard with no confirmation. Did it go through? A person checks their email, or refreshes, or calls someone. An agent has to decide whether the task is done, and if the interface doesn’t say so clearly, it can’t. In my last piece for UX Collective I argued that trust in financial products lives in moments like this. Agents make the same argument from the other side: a task isn’t complete until the interface tells you it is.

We’ve seen this before: the curb-cut effect

None of this is new territory. It’s accessibility.

Many of the fixes that help agents are the same ones that help people using screen readers, keyboard navigation, or magnification: real text labels instead of icon-only buttons, states that are announced instead of implied, predictable structure, no content that only exists on hover. The WebAIM Million report has documented year after year how common these basic gaps are across the web’s most visited homepages.

Angela Glover Blackwell called this pattern the curb-cut effect: design for people with specific constraints, and you end up improving things for everyone. Curb cuts were built for wheelchairs and are used by every parent with a stroller. Clear labels and visible state were required for assistive technology, and they help every user who’s tired, rushed, or new.

Agents are, in a sense, the newest constrained user. They push in the same direction accessibility advocates have been pushing for decades, which is a welcome thing. The work that makes a portal legible to an agent is largely the work we should have done for people already.

Where the analogy breaks

It would be too clean to say “design for agents and humans benefit.” Three places it gets complicated:

Some friction is supposed to be there. I’ve written before about graduated ceremony: matching the weight of a confirmation to the consequence of the action. Some steps exist precisely to slow things down. A confirmation before moving money, a second check before deleting an account. Making those steps “agent-friendly” by removing them would be a mistake. The better answer is to design for delegation explicitly: let a person grant an agent specific, limited authority up front, so the ceremony happens at the moment of handoff rather than disappearing altogether.

Not every site wants agents. CAPTCHAs and bot detection exist for real reasons: fraud, scraping, abuse. Some services have a legitimate interest in knowing whether a human is present. “Agent-legible” and “agent-permitted” are different questions, and designers will increasingly have to answer the second one deliberately rather than by accident.

Agents also fail where people don’t. They can misread a visually dense layout a person would parse instantly, or miss context a human gets from the surrounding page. So agent failures aren’t a perfect proxy for human failures. They’re a strong signal, not a verdict. When an agent and a person both struggle in the same place, that overlap is where I’d look first.

Using agents as a usability lens

You don’t need to build for agents to learn from them. A few questions I now ask in every design review, whether or not an agent will ever touch the screen:

  • Could someone who can’t guess complete this? If the path depends on trying both buttons, it’s a labeling problem.
  • Is every state visible without hovering, remembering, or color alone?
  • Does success announce itself? If the only proof a task finished is that nothing went wrong, it hasn’t been designed yet.
  • Does each interruption earn its place? If it would stop a machine, it’s costing your users more than you think.
  • Does this flow survive a real task’s length? Timeouts designed for a single quick visit break every longer process, human or not.

For years, usability testing meant recruiting people and watching them muddle through. That’s still irreplaceable. But there’s now a second kind of tester showing up on our interfaces, one that never muddles, never guesses, and never quietly absorbs our mistakes. The places it gets stuck are a map of the design debt we’ve been asking people to carry.

Trust has always lived in the details. Agents just stopped letting us get away with skipping them.

References and further reading

  • Steve Krug, Don’t Make Me Think
  • Don Norman on signifiers, The Design of Everyday Things
  • Jakob Nielsen, “10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design”
  • WebAIM Million annual accessibility report
  • Angela Glover Blackwell, “The Curb-Cut Effect,” Stanford Social Innovation Review
  • “The hidden UX of payments” in the UX Collective

title: What I learned teaching AI prototyping at university
text:
What I learned teaching AI prototyping at university

Teaching students how to prototype with AI tools instead of Figma revealed exciting possibilities and uncomfortable trade-offs. It also offered valuable insight into how non-tech people can create apps with generative AI.

I teach digital prototyping to fashion design undergraduates and master’s students at UPM’s Fashion School. My course focuses on exploring app concepts that can enrich the fashion experience. Past project ideas ranged from aesthetic affinity social communities (and dating) and live-action fashion-branded games to smart garment upcycling, VR fashion recommendations, and even a shared laundry app for roommates.

In previous semesters, I asked my students to prototype in Figma and standard design software. This past term, however, we switched to an entirely AI-based toolset, including Google Stitch, Google AI Studio, and Lovable.

The main reason for this change was, as Philip van Allen anticipated in his pre-LLM paper, that new AI design tools (such as Lovable or Bolt) would be much better suited to explore dynamic, interactive behaviors and flows than classic static screen-based design tools like Figma (in its 2025 version). Precious Ogar discusses the approach in more detail in his article AI-Focused Prototyping: A Practical Guide for UI/UX Designers.

The impact of this shift went beyond what I had anticipated and brought a new set of challenges. For starters, generative AI changed the very notion of prototyping: we were no longer building interconnected mockups to simulate an experience, but creating dynamic, functional applications that felt much closer to real products.

More importantly, it also changed how students practiced design skills and thought about product design — potentially for the worse. Greater reliance on tools meant less time spent conceptualizing. Endless prompting and refining replaced the hands-on practice required to master foundational design skills. And those skills are still highly relevant to creating production-quality experiences.

Yet, the final outcome gave my students the genuine confidence that they could build AI-enabled apps themselves — something I find deeply satisfying, and believe to be true.

In the end, the experience convinced me that prototyping with this new generation of tools demands a new kind of design literacy — one that puts more emphasis on thinking about our design than on the mechanics of building it.

Below are some of the key lessons I learned while teaching AI prototyping to fashion design students. They are presented in no particular order and vary in scope and relevance, but I believe each offers valuable insights for educators and designers.

What are we building?

Traditionally, a prototype was just a set of interactive mockups — a quick, low-effort way to test a concept without building an MVP or real app.

But GenAI has blurred that boundary. Today, anybody can create a partially working app in roughly the same time. And because these apps are made up of actual JavaScript and HTML code, they can include real features like live user authentication, persistent storage, and support all types of business logic. In other words, you are creating a conventional web app instead of a classic prototype.

But this impressive capability created a conceptual trap for my students. Many assumed the apps they were creating would inherently possess the same ‘magical’ AI capabilities as the tools used to build them. Some even saw these tools as oracles, as Olmanson et al. observed in their research with design students.

They expected their prototypes to be able to recognize images, perform semantic searches, or generate videos out of the box. They seemingly ignored that GenAI tools generate conventional web apps. Adding true AI functionality required significant setup work that was well beyond our class’s scope

I had to address this misconception directly in the classroom. I needed students to understand what they were building and where its limits were. When their concepts demanded complex AI capabilities, I guided them back to the fundamentals of prototyping: simulate the experience using mockups, predefined states, and pre-generated media.

Even in the age of AI, the golden rule of prototyping still holds: fake it, don’t make it.

The product vision is yours

Inevitably, most students began prototyping with high-level, generic prompts. And they were quickly disappointed by the results. It wasn’t just the visuals or interactions, but the product itself that didn’t match their expectations.

When I asked students to describe the product they wanted to build, it soon became clear that most couldn’t picture it themselves. So I asked them to develop a clearer vision of what they wanted to build. Starting from the home page, write down what information the product would show to the user, and what it would allow them to do. And then, determine the top sections of the app and repeat the same exercise for each.

Once they worked that out, they made much faster progress because they could communicate their intent much more clearly.

The conceptual model is yours too

This leads directly to the next challenge. When it came to specifying detailed app behavior and flows, a recurring challenge was mental model misalignment. Even when students had a clearer idea of how their product should work, AI tools frequently generated something completely different from their intent. Those alternatives could be perfectly reasonable. But they just weren’t right for the product the students were trying to build.

Help came when we discussed how to specify high-level design aspects for their apps. I introduced them to mental models and conceptual models. In a couple of cases, we applied very rudimentary conceptual grammars (mapping out objects, attributes, actions, and relationships). These allowed to map the users' mental models into their apps more effectively and helped the students to prompt more confidently the detailed behaviour they expected from their products.

This lesson also extends to professional designers as well. Generative AI excels at providing average solutions for conventional problems. But if you are designing something complex, novel, or off the beaten path, AI will likely default to standard patterns and miss your intent. To design effectively with AI, having a clear conceptual model is non-negotiable.

Prompting can be intimidating

Because everyone uses apps daily, at first, my students assumed that describing one to an AI tool would be easy. It seemed almost too simple. But after their first few rounds of prompting, that confidence quickly gave way to frustration. The results often fell short of their expectations, and in some cases the outputs were completely different from what they had intended. A similar perception was observed by Olmanson et al. in their research work.

To help, I suggested using LLMs to refine their prompts before feeding them into the prototyping tools. This worked well in some cases. However, a few students ended up endlessly polishing prompts in ChatGPT or Gemini instead of testing them in the actual vibe-coding tool. For some, prompt refinement became a way to avoid confronting the prototype itself.

At that point, I had to remind them that iteration is about improving and evaluating the prototype, the tool’s output, not endlessly perfecting the prompt.

Design vocabulary is essential

One thing that consistently improved the quality of the results was using standard design vocabulary. When students described interfaces in everyday language, the outputs were often mediocre or inconsistent. Once they started using established design terms — such as button group, navigation menu, card, accordion, modal dialog, or splash screen — the AI became much more precise. The same was true for common UI behaviour terms like transition, persistence, overlay, scroll, and animation. And in certain cases, some basic software development vocabulary also proved useful.

This makes a lot of sense since the internal currency of AI tools is language. The more precise our vocabulary, the better they can understand what elements make up an interface and how those elements should behave and respond to user interactions.

Azamnouri et al. (2026) set up a similar AI educational project and also found that their students needed to acquire certain technical capabilities to successfully prototype their app ideas.

English produced better results

Our classes took place in Madrid, and most students naturally wrote their prompts in Spanish. While this was not in any way a controlled study, we noticed that prompts written in English often appeared to produce more accurate results and soon became a practical consideration in class.

This may reflect an implicit bias in AI tools, partly because so much of the material used to train them is in English. And if we see this effect with Spanish, one of the world’s most widely spoken languages, the gap could be even wider for languages with far fewer online resources, such as Catalan or Macedonian. Language support raises a real inclusive design challenge for AI tools.

The value of element targeting

This might seem a minor point, but it offers a very practical lesson. Students often struggled to control the scope of their refinements. The tools would frequently apply modifications well beyond what the students had intended. This reflects how prompting, by its own descriptive nature, doesn’t make it easy to define a precise scope.

Luckily, most modern AI design tools allow you to select a specific on-screen element -a card, button, image, or section- as the target for your prompt.

That small interaction made a big difference. By narrowing the scope before prompting, students got more accurate results and ran into far fewer headaches. It also reinforced an important principle of working with AI: the clearer the context, the better the outcome.

Pricing is an educational problem

Pricing was an important constraint. While preparing the course, I contacted several AI companies, including Lovable, Base44, and Claude, to ask about academic pricing. There were no class-specific plans available, and their standard plans were both expensive and unpredictable for a course where students need to explore freely. Unfortunately, under these conditions, my university denied funding.

This is a serious limitation. Exploration is not an optional part of design education. Students need room to try ideas, make mistakes, discard approaches, and start again. Credit-based pricing in educational settings clearly penalizes that type of experimentation.

Google’s vibe suite

As a result, we ended up using Google’s AI design products extensively, as they offered the most generous and comprehensive free plans. We were going to use Google Stitch anyway. It is Google’s vibe design tool and is particularly valuable for the broad exploration of both visual and interaction concepts, which are essential in the early stages of rapid prototyping. Once a clear direction emerged, students moved on to Google AI Studio, a proper vibe coding tool, to build interactive apps and flesh out their ideas.

On the downside, we did run into some significant performance issues, particularly with Google AI Studio. Our classes took place in the evenings in Madrid (CET), which coincides with morning and central business hours in the US. I can only speculate that we were hitting a period of peak demand for these tools.

Vibe coding is a QA nightmare

Prototyping with AI tools pushed students to adopt a tactic more commonly associated with software development: regression testing.

Modifying a feature in Google AI Studio often alters another part of the app that has already been completed. A new addition could change a layout, break a flow, remove a feature, or modify something that did not seem connected with the prompt. After a few of these incidents, students learned that every important change required a broader review. They had to test the whole app again, not only the feature they had just modified. Also, version bookmarking and history were very helpful in handling some catastrophic updates smoothly.

While code dependencies can partly explain this behaviour, sometimes it seemed quite random. Either way, this is currently the rather frustrating reality of vibe coding that app creators have to deal with.

Is AI prototyping slower?

This was the most shocking outcome of the course. Overall, it took my students slightly longer to create a prototype with AI tools than with Figma.

The reason probably lies in the fact that they were actually building something closer to a complete application rather than an app façade with some interactions, as is typically the case with traditional prototyping.

While vibe coding tools can produce incredible results in the matter of minutes, the process of creating a fully functional prototype clearly involves more decision-making, more debugging, and more testing. It also required students to develop a deeper understanding of the product they were trying to prototype.

AI and designer deskilling

By far, the most concerning lesson was related to the educational experience. Students using AI tools were able to create richer, more complete experiences. They explored more ambitious product concepts and even built working apps. Things that simply weren’t possible using Figma alone.

However, this also meant fewer opportunities to practise core UI design skills like arranging layouts, establishing visual hierarchy by means of size, color, and spacing, or grouping elements by applying the Gestalt principles. In comparison, my previous student cohorts, who used conventional prototyping tools, undoubtedly developed stronger competences in these key areas.

Perhaps, as Lee et al. (2025) evidenced in their work, relying on generative AI tools reduces users' cognitive processes and critical thinking. In the end, this effect may contribute to achieving lower skill levels. Similar concerns were expressed by Slava Polonski in his article “AI skill atrophy: Are we forgetting how to think?”

There is an uncomfortable paradox here. We are currently witnessing how the product designer role is shifting towards a higher level of involvement in the design process, with practitioners potentially being displaced from more tedious UI work. Yet to effectively supervise a design, designers still need a strong grasp of the fundamentals to identify and correct any problems in AI-generated outputs, whether they are conceptual, visual, or related to interaction.

On the other hand, we are facing the possibility of degrading our students’ core design skills. These have traditionally been acquired through hands-on practice with tools such as Figma. The temptation now is to divert curricular time towards AI-based design practice. This creates a real risk of deskilling the very people who will soon be called upon to provide oversight of AI-generated output.

There is a clear implication for design education. We cannot replace core skill learning with AI-based tool practice. But neither can we disregard AI-based design practice because of its enormous potential. Our challenge is to integrate both types of learning into the curriculum to prepare our students for their future role as AI designers.

Final thoughts

Replacing Figma with AI tools turned out to be about more than just speeding up prototyping. It changed the nature of what students were actually building. Instead of creating only the façade of an experience, they were able to build functional applications that could look surprisingly close to real products. A key takeaway was that students need to understand what AI tools are actually creating, how and when to incorporate AI-related features, and when a convincing simulation is a better choice.

The students who made the most progress were the ones who developed a clear product vision and some form of a conceptual model. Being able to explain what their product should show and how it should behave turned them into more effective builders. Design vocabulary, prompting in English, targeting specific elements, and limited refinement of prompts in LLMs proved useful in most cases.

At the same time, this experience also revealed a less attractive side to vibe coding. Building a functional prototype requires more decisions, testing, and debugging than creating a conventional interactive mockup. That often means more effort and time. Credit-based pricing and unreliable performance also limited the exploratory work that our course relies on. And because AI tools handle much of the detailed UI work, students spent less time practising the visual and interaction-design fundamentals they may need in the future.

This is the core takeaway for design educators. We need to preserve the hands-on practice through which students develop design fundamentals, while teaching them how to use AI tools responsibly and effectively. We cannot treat these as competing approaches: students need both.

Despite all these drawbacks, I found the final outcome genuinely encouraging. My students left the course feeling capable of turning a product idea into an MVP app by themselves. I believe that confidence, colored by the understanding of the possibilities and limitations of these tools, was the most valuable thing they gained.
